message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is the last common ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria**.  

- **Laurasiatheria** is a major group of placental mammals that includes the orders Carnivora (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and Perissodactyla (horses, rhinos, tapirs).  
- The most recent common ancestor of these two orders lived in the **Paleocene epoch**, roughly **70–80 million years ago**.  
- This ancestor was a small, insectivorous mammal that gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.

So, while lions and zebras diverged long ago, their most recent shared ancestor is that Paleocene Laurasiatherian mammal.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. We need to answer. The question is about evolutionary biology. Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga). They belong to different families: lions are Felidae (cat family), zebras are Equidae (horse family). Both are mammals, order Carnivora vs order Perissodactyla? Actually zebra is an odd-toed ungulate (Perissodactyla). Lions are carnivores (Carnivora). So their common ancestor would be at the level of mammals, perhaps the last common ancestor of placental mammals. But maybe they want the common ancestor at the level of the last common ancestor of the two species, which is the last common ancestor of the Felidae and Equidae. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lion and zebra would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a placental mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species, which is the last common ancestor of the two orders: Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would have been a small, insectivorous mammal that lived in the Paleocene. So answer: the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria, a small, insectivorous mammal that lived ~70-80 million years ago.

Alternatively, if we want to be more precise: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor likely lived in the Paleocene epoch, about 70-80 million years ago. It was a small, insectivorous mammal.

Thus answer: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, a small insectivorous mammal from the Paleocene. Or we can say: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor lived about 70-80 million years ago.

We can also mention that the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~100-120 million years ago). But the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. So answer accordingly.
